transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Yates (Redwood AE), Miguel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Lina Park (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (Redwood CSM); Mark Jensen (CTO, Lumen Health), Priya Singh (Eng Manager), Tom Wu (SRE), Asha Patel (Compliance), Diego Ramos (ML Eng)

Auto-summary (auto generated, may be partial): Discussed SLO composition, measurement plan, traffic sampling, and next steps for a 6-week POC. Decided on hybrid SLO approach, Redwood to run bench harness on sample data, customer to provide traffic.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sarah Yates: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll give a quick agenda. I'll kick off, miguel will do the technical dive, and then open q and a. can everyone hear ok?
[00:12] Mark Jensen: yep, loud and clear. thanks Sarah. we wanted to focus today on how we actually measure success - like first token latency matters for UI snappiness but overall request time matters for billing and downstream services.
[00:27] Miguel Ortiz: totally. so we usually break this into TTFT, first token time, and TPOT, total per token. TTFT is the user-perceived latency; TPOT captures per-token cost and throughput. there are tradeoffs.
[00:41] Priya Singh: quick question, we've been using a hosted API for most experiments. our main question is what thresholds we should commit to in a PoC without over-provisioning. p95 vs p99?
[00:56] Miguel Ortiz: good one. our recommendation for interactive chat workloads is a hybrid: set TTFT p95 target tighter (e.g., < 300ms) and TPOT p99 a bit looser depending on tokens per request. but for Lumen's domain (clinical summaries) payload sizes vary - we should tailor.
[01:14] Diego Ramos: when you say tokens per request, our average payload is 120 tokens but there are long cases hitting 1k tokens for discharge notes. it's the tail that worries us.
[01:27] Miguel Ortiz: right, that's typical. for tails we do two things: traffic sampling with stratified buckets (short, medium, long) and run burst/long-case benchmarks. we'll also recommend KV cache + prefix caching to reduce repeated prefix cost.
[01:42] Tom Wu: running KV cache is fine but network and VPC constraints matter. do you require egress, and how will IP allowlisting work during the PoC?
[01:53] Lina Park: we can run Redwood Private in your VPC for the PoC if needed; but for speed we usually do hosted with an IP allowlist or customer-managed VPC peering. we'll note action item to confirm.
[02:08] Asha Patel: compliance question - we need audit logs retained 1 year and KMS integration for any keys. will that be part of the PoC?
[02:18] Evan Brooks: we can include extended audit log retention as an add-on and show KMS integration in the private deployment docs. for the POC acceptance you won't need full production retention but we'll demo it.
[02:29] Sarah Yates: okay jumping into SLO specifics. miguel do you want to sketch a sample acceptance matrix?
[02:35] Miguel Ortiz: sure. so think of a matrix with segments: interactive (<=200 tokens), medium (200-600), long (>600). for each segment we propose TTFT p95 targets and TPOT p99 targets. example starting points for Lumen:
[02:52] Miguel Ortiz: interactive: TTFT p95 < 250ms, TPOT p99 per-token latency < 20ms; medium: TTFT p95 < 450ms, TPOT p99 < 30ms; long: TTFT p95 < 900ms, TPOT p99 < 50ms. these are conservative given mixed hardware.
[03:14] Priya Singh: those look aggressive for our current infra. are these assuming GPU pool, quantization, or specific sequence lengths?
[03:21] Miguel Ortiz: assumes quantized model (8-bit or 4-bit where applicable), continuous batching disabled for TTFT-critical paths, and a dedicated GPU pool for benchmarking. we'll show both dedicated and hosted numbers in the run.
[03:36] Mark Jensen: how do we measure TPOT exactly? is that per-token after first token or total request time divided by token count?
[03:43] Miguel Ortiz: good clarification - TPOT here is average per-token generation time measured during steady-state generation phase (excluding decode prep and network overhead). for acceptance we'll also track end-to-end request time (edge to model) as a separate metric.
[03:59] Diego Ramos: can you capture p99 of TPOT? p99 per-token seems noisy for long outputs.
[04:05] Miguel Ortiz: it is noisy, which is why we stratify by payload. for long outputs we expect wider variance; so for long segment we focus on TTFT p95 and TPOT p95 and use p99 as a risk indicator.
[04:18] Sarah Yates: real talk - customers often want both p95 and p99. for PoC acceptance, let's pick TTFT p95 and TPOT p99 for interactive and medium, and TTFT p95 + TPOT p95 for long. that balances tail sensitivity and noisy metrics.
[04:33] Priya Singh: ok that feels pragmatic. what about traffic sampling? how do we ensure the benchmark reflects production patterns?
[04:40] Miguel Ortiz: we ask for a 48-hour sample trace with request timestamps, token counts, and payload categories. Redwood has a replay harness that replays at scale with the same inter-arrival distribution. we also recommend a synthetic burst profile to emulate spikes.
[04:55] Tom Wu: can the replay harness preserve IP and header differences? our system routes based on tenant headers and has strict routing.
[05:03] Lina Park: yes, we can map or drop headers; we typically replace auth headers with a stub and preserve routing keys. we'll coordinate on required fields.
[05:13] Mark Jensen: timeline wise what's realistic for a 6-week PoC?
[05:18] Sarah Yates: week 0 - kickoff and traffic handoff; week 1 - dry run and config; week 2-3 - benchmark runs and SLO measurement; week 4 - tuning and re-run; week 5 - compile results and whiteboard wrap; week 6 - final review and decision.
[05:33] Priya Singh: who signs off on acceptance? is it SRE or product?
[05:36] Mark Jensen: ops (Tom) plus product (Priya) and security (Asha) will sign. so we'll need a clear acceptance checklist.
[05:45] Evan Brooks: we'll provide a PoC acceptance template that maps metrics to owners and allowable exception windows.
[05:51] Diego Ramos: on the topic of fallback - suppose the model variant fails or a node goes down, what's Redwood's recommended fallback?
[05:59] Miguel Ortiz: automatic model fallback to a smaller, faster quantized variant is a standard. also region fallback and queue-based graceful degradation where we return partial results with a hint (e.g., continue generation async). we'll show failover latencies.
[06:12] Tom Wu: for audit we need proof that fallback happened and why. are the logs granular enough?
[06:18] Lina Park: yes, we emit trace events for routing decisions, fallback triggers, and node health. those can be exported to your observability stack.
[06:26] Asha Patel: about data residency - some records cannot leave region. can we do a private deployment for the long-form cases only?
[06:34] Miguel Ortiz: yes, a hybrid deployment is possible. sensitive workloads can be routed to Private while less sensitive to Hosted. we can demo routing policies in the PoC.
[06:45] Sarah Yates: ok quick note on benchmarks: we'll run both cold-start (cache empty) and warmed cache runs, measure first token and per-token rates, and collect memory/CPU/GPU metrics.
[06:58] Mark Jensen: any thought on sampling frequency for p99 estimation? we worry about long collection periods to get stable p99.
[07:06] Miguel Ortiz: recommended approach: sample over multiple windows (5, 15, 60 minutes) and stitch p99 using tail aggregation. we'll use bootstrapping to estimate confidence intervals. for the PoC we'll provide both raw samples and aggregated metrics.
[07:21] Priya Singh: can you include cost modelling? we need to understand projected token costs at scale and effect of quantization on quality.
[07:28] Sarah Yates: yes, Redwood Optimize team will produce a simple cost model and a quality regression test over your eval prompts. we'll include quantization variants and expected cost delta.
[07:38] Diego Ramos: about quality regressions - can we run an automated eval against 200 golden examples?
[07:44] Lina Park: absolutely - send your golden examples. we'll run automatic rouge/bertscore plus human sampling for edge cases.
[07:51] Miguel Ortiz: one more technical note: when measuring TTFT we try to remove client-side serialization overhead by instrumenting at the edge or using a small client harness. please expect small differences vs in-app measurements.
[08:02] Tom Wu: that's fine as long as we can correlate traces. we'll need tracer ids attached.
[08:08] Sarah Yates: let's capture decisions and owners now.
[08:12] Sarah Yates: Decision 1: hybrid SLO composition (TTFT p95 + TPOT p99 for interactive/medium, TTFT p95 + TPOT p95 for long). Owner: Redwood + Lumen engineering.
[08:24] Sarah Yates: Decision 2: 48-hour sample traffic and 100 golden prompts to be provided by Lumen. Owner: Diego Ramos.
[08:33] Sarah Yates: Decision 3: Redwood to deliver benchmark harness, initial run, and PoC acceptance template. Owner: Miguel Ortiz / Sarah.
[08:43] Mark Jensen: agreed. a few more Qs - what's the rollback path if we can't meet SLOs?
[08:49] Miguel Ortiz: rollback options: increase capacity temporarily (burst), fallback to smaller model with degradation statement, or change routing to queued async processing. all of these will be in the runbook.
[08:59] Priya Singh: and if quality drops with quantization?
[09:03] Miguel Ortiz: we'll include quality regression thresholds; if any variant produces >X% drop on your golden set we'll reject it for production. the PoC will measure quality in parallel.
[09:12] Asha Patel: final compliance note - please provide SOC2 and ISO docs and a pointer to your encryption whitepaper.
[09:18] Evan Brooks: we'll circulate our compliance pack after the call.
[09:22] Sarah Yates: ok closing - we'll follow up with artifacts. thanks everyone.
[09:28] Mark Jensen: thanks, very helpful.
[09:31] End of transcript (approx).
notes: Customer emphasized tail behavior and mixed payloads; agreed to hybrid SLO. PoC will demonstrate both latency and quality tradeoffs across quantized variants.
